origin.fact: Captive-bred colour strain of the common guppy. It is not a separate species, has no wild form and is not related to koi carp.
The name describes a look borrowed from koi carp (red or orange on white, sometimes with black). It is a trade pattern name, not an origin, and no breeder or date is documented.
One Vietnamese article says breeders in Thailand and Malaysia developed the pattern in the 1990s through many generations of selection. This claim is unverified.
Most Koi guppies sold in Vietnam come from Thailand and are imported by hobbyists and shops.

looks.fact: Pale or white body with sharp red or orange blocks on the head, back and/or tail.
Many lines are built on an albino or translucent base. A clean red head or tail needs careful selection, because the colour can break into patchy orange.
Kohaku factor: both sexes have a red head, red tail and red back.
Vietnamese hobbyists describe it as an albino line with red eyes, a white body and a red head and tail.
A good fish shows sharp red-on-white contrast, intact fins and clear eyes.
Breeders do not share one fixed standard for the pattern.

lines.fact: Red koi: red or orange blocks on white, the most common form. Red Cap: red mostly on the head. White koi: mostly white with small red marks. Golden or blonde koi: the pattern on a golden base. Albino koi: red eyes and a pinkish-white body. Tiger koi: black tiger stripes on the tail or rear half.
Kohaku Koi Tuxedo: Kohaku red head and tail plus a black Tuxedo rear body. Often combined with Elephant Ear (Dumbo), where males have enlarged, coloured pectoral fins.
Koi Tuxedo comes in standard-fin and Dumbo Ear forms. Only Dumbo Ear males grow the big pectoral fins; females carry the gene but look normal.
Koi Red Tuxedo Red Nose is sold as a high-end strain.
Lines named in Vietnam: Albino Koi (red-eyed), black Koi, King Koi, Koi Red Ear and Koi Ribbon.
Koi Cobra combines the koi colours with a snakeskin (cobra) pattern.

keeping.fact: A 10-gallon (about 38 L) tank suits a trio; 20 gallons is better for five or more fish. Use a sponge filter or a filter with gentle flow to protect long fins.
Hard, stable water is preferred. Avoid soft or acidic water such as tanks with driftwood or peat.
A 40x30x30 cm tank holds about 5–7 pairs. Change 20–40% of the water each week and let tap water stand 1–2 days first.
Feed small pellets as the staple. Carotenoid foods with astaxanthin or spirulina help keep the red. Add brine shrimp and daphnia as treats.
Vietnamese keepers feed live foods (tubifex, moina, Artemia, mosquito larvae) together with Thai or Japanese pellets to bring out colour.

Good tankmates are corydoras, small rasboras and tetras, otocinclus and snails. Avoid fin-nippers, bettas, large cichlids, goldfish and koi carp, and keep them apart from Endler's livebearers, which hybridise with guppies.
Pale-bodied fish show stress quickly when water quality drops.

breeding.fact: Livebearer. Gestation is about 4–6 weeks, with broods of usually 20–40 fry. Females can store sperm for 6 months or more.

Not true-breeding. The koi colour depends on several genes and drifts without selection, so keeping the pattern needs culling and new unrelated stock. Tiger lines and Endler crosses give mixed offspring.
Females give birth every 28–35 days. Dense plants such as Java moss or guppy grass help fry survive.
Large females can drop 120–150 fry. Adults eat fry, so use a breeding box or thick plants.

health.fact: Common problems are Camallanus worms, internal parasites, fin rot and fungus. Inbreeding can weaken immunity, so bring in new stock every few generations.
Commonly reported: white spot (ich), fin rot and velvet.
Stress (fish sitting in a corner) is common after moving. Acclimate new fish slowly.

buying.fact: Pick active fish with clear eyes and even colour. Avoid washed-out juveniles that were sold too young.
Look for sharp red-white contrast and intact fins. Avoid tanks holding any sick fish, ask for line history if you plan to breed, quarantine new fish and drip-acclimate them.
In Vietnam, prices run from about 40,000 VND a pair to several million VND, depending on the line.

controversy.fact: The name 'koi' has no fixed standard. Similar fish are sold as Kohaku or under other names, so the label alone does not guarantee a stable line.
